rows: Hepatitis B is a blood-borne viral infection.
Acute and chronic infection require appropriate clinical assessment.
Laboratory markers distinguish infection status and infectivity.
Relevant cases are notifiable under health-protection arrangements.
Contacts may require testing and vaccination or post-exposure management.
Vaccination is available for people at increased risk.
Pregnancy screening and newborn prophylaxis reduce vertical transmission.
Surveillance supports prevention, treatment and elimination planning.
A positive single marker or risk factor does not define the full hepatitis B status.
Conclusions require marker pattern, timing, symptoms, exposure, vaccination, treatment and specialist evidence.
Hepatitis C is a blood-borne viral infection.
Antibody testing indicates exposure but does not by itself prove current infection.
RNA testing is used to identify active infection.
Direct-acting antiviral treatment can cure most treated infections.
People with relevant exposure risks should have access to testing.
Needle and equipment sharing are important preventable transmission routes.
Testing and treatment data identify gaps in the care pathway.
Surveillance supports progress toward eliminating hepatitis C as a public-health threat.
A positive antibody result or historic exposure does not prove current hepatitis C infection.
Conclusions require antibody, RNA, timing, exposure, treatment and follow-up evidence.
Tetanus is caused by toxin produced by Clostridium tetani.
Routine vaccination is the main preventive measure.
Wound assessment should consider contamination, tissue damage and vaccination history.
Tetanus-prone and high-risk wounds may require specific prophylaxis.
Vaccination should be brought up to date when indicated.
Tetanus immunoglobulin may be required for specified high-risk circumstances.
Suspected clinical tetanus requires urgent specialist management.
Cases contribute to national surveillance and prevention review.
A dirty wound or incomplete recollection of vaccination does not by itself determine prophylaxis.
Decisions require wound type, timing, immunisation records, immune status and current UKHSA guidance.
Psittacosis is caused by Chlamydia psittaci.
Human infection is commonly associated with infected birds.
Inhalation of contaminated dust or droplets is an important exposure route.
Illness can include fever, headache and respiratory symptoms.
Diagnosis can be supported by PCR testing of suitable respiratory samples.
Bird and occupational exposure histories are important.
Clusters should prompt coordinated human, animal and environmental investigation.
Bird ownership or pneumonia does not establish psittacosis.
Conclusions require exposure, symptoms, specimen, laboratory, treatment and epidemiological evidence.
